patient.chief_complaint: Sudden loss of consciousness and fall at home
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Eleanor Marsh is a 74-year-old woman with a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (on metoprolol and diltiazem for rate control), hypertension, and hypothyroidism who was brought to the emergency department by her daughter after a witnessed syncopal episode at home. Her daughter reports that her mother was standing in the kitchen preparing tea at approximately 8:40 AM when she abruptly went pale, slumped against the counter, and fell to the floor. She was unresponsive for approximately 12 to 15 seconds. Her eyes were closed and she appeared limp, with no tonic stiffening, no rhythmic limb jerking, and no facial twitching. She regained consciousness spontaneously, was immediately coherent and oriented, and asked what had happened. She had no confusion, no headache, and no post-event drowsiness. There was no tongue biting and no urinary or fecal incontinence. The patient herself recalls feeling entirely well moments before, with no preceding chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath. She does recall a brief fleeting sensation of lightheadedness and graying of her peripheral vision for approximately 2 to 3 seconds immediately before losing consciousness. Over the past six to eight weeks she has experienced three prior near-syncopal spells, each lasting a few seconds, during which her vision grayed and she felt as though she was about to black out, but she did not fall. These episodes have occurred both at rest and with mild exertion such as rising from a chair. She has also noticed increased fatigue and occasional palpitations, which she attributes to her known atrial fibrillation. She has had no fever, recent illness, vomiting, or diarrhea. She denies chest pain at rest, dyspnea, or lower extremity swelling. Her most recent thyroid check approximately eight months ago was reported as within normal limits. She has been on dual rate-control therapy with both metoprolol and diltiazem for approximately 18 months, started after her AF was perceived to be difficult to control with metoprolol alone. Her last cardiology visit was approximately one year ago and she had been doing well until the recent spells began.

output.impression: 48-hour Holter monitoring demonstrates predominantly sinus rhythm with sinus bradycardia (nadir 34 bpm). Three episodes of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation were captured; the longest lasted 22 minutes. At spontaneous termination of this AF episode, a sinus pause of 4.8 seconds was documented before sinus rhythm resumed. This pause is symptom-correlated: the patient-activated event marker and diary entry ('felt dizzy and blacked out briefly') coincide precisely with the 4.8-second pause at 09:36 on day 2. Two additional asymptomatic sinus pauses of 2.1 and 2.4 seconds were documented. No sustained ventricular tachycardia. Rare isolated PVCs (22 total). The recording is consistent with a tachy-brady pattern.

output.query: sick sinus syndrome sinus node dysfunction syncope pacemaker indications

results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Syncope
results.authors: Brignole M, Moya A, de Lange FJ, et al.
results.summary: Cardiac syncope due to intrinsic sinus node dysfunction (sick sinus syndrome), including the tachy-brady variant, is a Class I indication for permanent pacing when symptoms correlate with documented bradycardia or pauses. A normal resting 12-lead ECG does not exclude paroxysmal sinus node dysfunction; prolonged ambulatory monitoring is essential to capture symptom-rhythm correlation.

results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Patients with Syncope
results.authors: Shen WK, Sheldon RS, Benditt DG, et al.
results.journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
results.summary: In patients with suspected arrhythmic syncope and a non-diagnostic resting ECG, ambulatory cardiac monitoring (Holter, event monitor, or implantable loop recorder) is recommended to establish symptom-rhythm correlation. Sinus pauses exceeding 3 seconds that are symptom-correlated constitute a Class I pacing indication.

results.title: External Prolonged Electrocardiographic Monitoring in Unexplained Syncope
results.authors: Locati ET, Moya A, Oliveira M, et al.
results.summary: Ambulatory ECG monitoring is the cornerstone of arrhythmia diagnosis in syncope. Holter monitoring is indicated when arrhythmic syncope is suspected; event monitors and implantable loop recorders extend diagnostic yield for infrequent events. Symptom-rhythm correlation during monitoring is required to confirm a causative arrhythmic mechanism.

output.summary: Sick sinus syndrome with symptom-correlated sinus pauses is a well-established cause of cardiac syncope. A normal resting ECG is common between episodes and does not exclude the diagnosis. Current ESC and ACC/AHA/HRS guidelines recommend ambulatory cardiac monitoring to capture symptom-rhythm correlation; a symptomatic sinus pause exceeding 3 seconds meets Class I criteria for permanent pacemaker implantation. Rate-slowing drugs (beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers) should be reviewed, as they can potentiate sinus node dysfunction.

output.proposed: Metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily + Diltiazem 120 mg daily (extended release) — current combination
interactions: Combination of beta-blocker (metoprolol) and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (diltiazem) produces additive depression of sinus node automaticity and AV nodal conduction
Each agent individually slows sinus rate; in combination, the effect is synergistic and may unmask or exacerbate underlying sinus node dysfunction
Diltiazem inhibits CYP3A4, increasing metoprolol plasma concentration by approximately 30-50%, further amplifying beta-blockade
contraindications: Concurrent use is relatively contraindicated in patients with pre-existing sinus node dysfunction or sick sinus syndrome without a functioning pacemaker
Should be avoided in symptomatic sinus bradycardia or recurrent sinus pauses without pacemaker protection
warnings: Monitor heart rate closely; sinus bradycardia, prolonged sinus pauses, and symptomatic syncope may result from this combination
Consider dose reduction or discontinuation of one or both agents in the setting of documented symptomatic sinus pauses
Apixaban: no pharmacokinetic interaction with metoprolol or diltiazem; dosing unaffected
alternatives: If rate control for AF is still required, consider digoxin at low doses (avoids direct sinus node suppression), or reassess rhythm control strategy
Beta-blocker or non-DHP CCB monotherapy at lowest effective dose following definitive pacing

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Cardiac syncope due to sick sinus syndrome (sinus node dysfunction)

differential.key_features: Near-normal resting ECG makes high-degree AV block less likely; monitoring excludes it by capturing sinus-origin pauses rather than blocked P waves.
No clear trigger, no prodrome of warmth or nausea; negative tilt-table; occurs both at rest and on mild exertion — atypical for vasovagal in a 74-year-old.
Dual sinus-node-suppressing agents are a reversible contributor that must be addressed alongside intrinsic sinus node dysfunction.
TSH normal on presentation; levothyroxine dose stable; does not explain paroxysmal pauses.

sequence_constraints.reason: ECG must be reviewed before disposition and specialist referral; drives admission decision and arrhythmia workup pathway.
Troponin assessment must precede monitoring strategy to exclude acute myocardial ischemia as a precipitant.
Structural assessment should precede specialist disposition to inform pacing suitability.

critical_actions: Admit to continuous cardiac telemetry to capture symptom-rhythm correlation
Obtain Holter or event monitoring to document sinus pauses and correlate with syncope
Review and hold or reduce sinus-node-suppressing drugs (metoprolol, diltiazem) in the setting of symptomatic sinus pauses
Refer to cardiology / electrophysiology for permanent pacemaker evaluation once symptomatic pause is documented
Counsel patient on driving restriction until syncope is evaluated and definitively treated
contraindicated_actions: Do not exclude arrhythmic syncope based on a near-normal or normal resting 12-lead ECG — paroxysmal sinus node dysfunction requires ambulatory monitoring to detect
Do not continue dual sinus-node-suppressing therapy (metoprolol + diltiazem) without pacemaker protection in a patient with documented symptomatic sinus pauses
Do not perform tilt-table testing as the primary diagnostic test when cardiac monitoring can establish symptom-rhythm correlation
Do not discharge home before symptom-rhythm correlation is established or an outpatient monitoring plan is in place
key_reasoning_points: Sick sinus syndrome (sinus node dysfunction) is a common cause of syncope in elderly patients and frequently presents with a near-normal resting ECG between paroxysmal events — a normal resting ECG does not exclude the diagnosis
The tachy-brady variant of sick sinus syndrome, with paroxysmal AF followed by prolonged post-conversion pauses, is a classic presentation and requires ambulatory monitoring to capture
A symptom-correlated sinus pause exceeding 3 seconds is a Class I indication for permanent pacemaker per both ESC and ACC/AHA/HRS guidelines

The combination of a beta-blocker and a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker produces additive and synergistic sinus node suppression; drug-induced bradycardia must be recognized as a potentially reversible contributor alongside intrinsic sinus node dysfunction
Cardiac monitoring — not tilt-table testing — is the key diagnostic tool when paroxysmal arrhythmic syncope is suspected

red_herrings.data_point: Near-normal resting ECG showing only sinus bradycardia at 48 bpm with no conduction disease
red_herrings.intended_effect: A naive clinician may be falsely reassured by the absence of high-degree block or obvious arrhythmia on the resting ECG and conclude that cardiac arrhythmia is unlikely, missing the paroxysmal nature of sinus node dysfunction.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A near-normal resting ECG does not exclude paroxysmal sinus node dysfunction; the diagnosis requires ambulatory monitoring to capture the intermittent sinus pause that is the actual cause of syncope.

clinical_pearls: Sick sinus syndrome frequently presents with a normal or near-normal resting ECG between paroxysmal events; diagnosis requires ambulatory monitoring
The tachy-brady syndrome (paroxysmal AF followed by post-conversion sinus arrest) is a classic SSS variant that can be missed on a single ECG snapshot
Dual rate-control therapy with a beta-blocker and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker potentiates sinus node suppression and can unmask or worsen underlying sinus node dysfunction
A symptomatic sinus pause exceeding 3 seconds is a Class I indication for permanent pacemaker implantation regardless of whether drug reduction is possible
